name: Yet Another Sorting Problem
description: Petya has an array of integers $$$a_1, a_2, \ldots, a_n$$$. He only likes sorted arrays. Unfortunately, the given array could be arbitrary, so Petya wants to sort it. Petya likes to challenge himself, so he wants to sort array using only $$$3$$$-cycles. More formally, in one operation he can pick $$$3$$$ pairwise distinct indices $$$i$$$, $$$j$$$, and $$$k$$$ ($$$1 \leq i, j, k \leq n$$$) and apply $$$i \to j \to k \to i$$$ cycle to the array $$$a$$$. It simultaneously places $$$a_i$$$ on position $$$j$$$, $$$a_j$$$ on position $$$k$$$, and $$$a_k$$$ on position $$$i$$$, without changing any other element. For example, if $$$a$$$ is $$$[10, 50, 20, 30, 40, 60]$$$ and he chooses $$$i = 2$$$, $$$j = 1$$$, $$$k = 5$$$, then the array becomes $$$[\underline{50}, \underline{40}, 20, 30, \underline{10}, 60]$$$. Petya can apply arbitrary number of $$$3$$$-cycles (possibly, zero). You are to determine if Petya can sort his array $$$a$$$, i. e. make it non-decreasing.
input_specification: Each test contains multiple test cases. The first line contains the number of test cases $$$t$$$ ($$$1 \leq t \leq 5 \cdot 10^5$$$). Description of the test cases follows. The first line of each test case contains a single integer $$$n$$$ ($$$1 \leq n \leq 5 \cdot 10^5$$$) — the length of the array $$$a$$$. The second line of each test case contains $$$n$$$ integers $$$a_1, a_2, \ldots, a_n$$$ ($$$1 \leq a_i \leq n$$$). It is guaranteed that the sum of $$$n$$$ over all test cases does not exceed $$$5 \cdot 10^5$$$.
output_specification: For each test case, print " YES " (without quotes) if Petya can sort the array $$$a$$$ using $$$3$$$-cycles, and " NO " (without quotes) otherwise. You can print each letter in any case (upper or lower).

approach_summary: Maintain prefix sums and dynamic point updates via Fenwick tree using lowbit operations (i & -i) in O(log N) time and O(N) space.

topic_editorial.title: Editorial: 1585D — Yet Another Sorting Problem [70. BIT / Fenwick Tree]
topic_editorial.summary: Point updates and range prefix queries with Fenwick Tree.
topic_editorial.key_invariant: Every integer $i$ has a unique binary decomposition. Index $i$ in a Binary Indexed Tree stores the cumulative sum of the interval $(i - \text{lowbit}(i), i]$, allowing logarithmic traversal via $i \mathrel{+}= (i \mathbin{\&} -i)$ and $i \mathrel{-}= (i \mathbin{\&} -i)$.
